source.version: arXiv:2503.01631v1 [cs.HC], 3 Mar 2025; typeset as the CHI '25 manuscript, DOI 10.1145/3706598.3713273 (PDF p. 1). This is the saved arXiv version; the ACM version of record was not compared.
source.supplement_used: Appendices A-E within the same PDF, pp. 17-25. No separate statistical supplement or data repository is identified in the document or available with this paper on file.

studies.label: Main online experiment (problem reframing, four conditions)

counts_source.locator: PDF p. 6, Figure 4 and Section 4.2; arm totals: PDF p. 9, Figure 8, right-hand table, Total column
counts_source.quote: We recruited 456 individuals by means of the two crowdsourcing platforms. [...] In the end, we had 280 participants

arms.name: MANUAL
arms.description: Designers reframe the assigned problem themselves, without an LLM (PDF p. 5, Figure 3 and Section 4).

arms.name: DIRECT
arms.description: A button sends fixed prompts to GPT-4o to generate or regenerate alternative frames; participants can submit or build on these frames. Role: ideas_supplied (PDF p. 6, Section 4.3; pp. 17-18, Appendix A.1).

arms.name: STRUCTURED
arms.description: A button-driven GPT-4o prompt chain implements Dorst’s nine-step reframing process, supplying intermediate content and final frames; participants can regenerate content or add their own. Role: ideas_supplied (PDF pp. 19-23, Appendix A.2).

arms.name: FREE-FORM
arms.description: Participants converse freely with default ChatGPT, using GPT-4o on their own account; conversation logs confirm use. Role: open_chat (PDF p. 7, Section 4.5).

studies.task: Designers reframe one assigned design problem about aging delivery drivers, cigarette-butt litter, or conflicting lunch preferences, produce two novel and useful alternative frames in a common template, and select their best frame for expert evaluation (PDF pp. 5-7, Sections 4-4.5; pp. 24-25, Appendix C).

ai_tool.name: OpenAI GPT-4o; default ChatGPT (GPT-4o) for FREE-FORM
ai_tool.locator: PDF p. 2, Section 1, identifies GPT-4o and dates the experiment to August 2024; PDF p. 7, Section 4.5, confirms the same model for FREE-FORM. The model release year is not explicitly printed.

preregistration.where: No preregistration is stated in the complete PDF.

estimates.outcome: Novelty of the participant’s selected problem frame (expert rated)
estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Fifteen designers selected from participants with high scores on the pre-task reframing quiz evaluated other participants’ selected frames (PDF p. 8, end of Section 4.5; p. 25, Table 11). Raters were blind to the production condition (PDF p. 5, Section 4.1). Each reviewed thirty-six randomly sampled frames spanning approaches and problems (PDF p. 6, Section 4.3). Questionnaires adapted from Doshi and Hauser asked how novel or useful each frame’s perspective was relative to the original problem description (PDF p. 7, Section 4.4). Figure 5 uses an axis from one to nine, but scale anchors, item aggregation, ratings per frame, and aggregation across raters are not stated. The expert_raters code follows the paper’s designation of these design practitioners.

sources.locator: PDF p. 8, Section 5, opening paragraph
sources.quote: We analyzed the 280 problem frames that participants selected as the best ones from their reframing.

sources.locator: PDF p. 8, Section 5, statistical-analysis paragraph
sources.quote: For this, we performed Mann–Whitney 𝑈testing, considering the imbalance in sample size between the groups.

sources.locator: PDF p. 8 continuing on PDF p. 9, Section 5.2; Figure 5, left panel
sources.quote: As Figure 5 shows, there were no statistically significant differences for either, between the manual and the llm-all group but also among all the individual approaches (all 𝑝> 0.05).

estimates.notes: Figure 5 (PDF p. 8) gives unlabeled box plots, with no printed arm means, SDs, SEs, differences, intervals, or effect sizes; no plot values were read off or digitized. The Figure 8 counts are printed table entries, recovered from the embedded font glyph codes and checked on a pymupdf-rendered page; the parenthesized values in those count-source rows are age means and SDs, not outcome dispersion. The paper analyzes each participant’s selected frame, but does not describe rating aggregation. The paper calls the combined AI arm llm-all. Its sole numeric outcome result is the shared all p > 0.05 bound for novelty and usefulness, also covering the across-approach analyses; no exact p-value or Mann–Whitney U statistic is printed. se_basis is participant because the stated analysis is one selected output per analyzed person; no SE or CI is printed, and the unreported rating aggregation prevents an independent check of the actual test input. The combined treatment includes both supplied-idea interfaces and open chat.

sources.quote: As Figure 5 shows, there were no statistically significant differences for either, between the manual and the llm-all group but also among all the individual approaches (all 𝑝> 0.05).

estimates.notes: Figure 5 (PDF p. 8) gives unlabeled box plots, with no printed arm means, SDs, SEs, differences, intervals, or effect sizes; no plot values were read off or digitized. The Figure 8 counts are printed table entries, recovered from the embedded font glyph codes and checked on a pymupdf-rendered page; the parenthesized values in those count-source rows are age means and SDs, not outcome dispersion. The paper analyzes each participant’s selected frame, but does not describe rating aggregation. This screening-map contrast is retained as a figure/qualitative record. The paper names Kruskal–Wallis testing across all approaches and Dunn’s test with Bonferroni correction as its general post-hoc procedure (PDF p. 8), but prints no result for this particular pair. The shared all p > 0.05 sentence is preserved in sources as context and is not assigned to a pair-specific p_value; p_value and test are null, and se_basis is not_reported. The pair total and the pair’s total output count are not printed; n_total and n_units remain null rather than summing arm counts.

open_items: For both eligible outcomes, arm means, outcome SDs, SEs, mean differences, confidence intervals, test-statistic values, and standardized effects are absent. Figure 5 contains no numeric labels for box-plot values. These records cannot supply a standardized effect from printed statistics.

No pair-specific novelty or usefulness test is printed. The shared all p > 0.05 statement covers the pooled AI-versus-MANUAL and across-approach analyses; it does not identify particular Dunn comparisons or establish their individual p-value bounds. Single-arm contrast statistics remain null.

The paper does not describe how multiple ratings were combined or the exact inputs to the nonparametric tests. The pooled records’ participant se_basis follows the stated analysis of one selected frame per person, but the actual independence treatment is not documented; no participant-level SE or CI is available.
Rating-scale anchors, number of questionnaire items, ratings per frame, and rater aggregation are unstated. The plot axis alone does not establish the full measurement protocol.

Per-arm randomized counts and exclusions are unreported. Post-assignment exclusions include AI-arm non-users, so the analyzed sample is not an intention-to-treat sample and differential attrition cannot be assessed.
No preregistration is stated. Novelty and usefulness are named in the primary hypothesis H1 (PDF p. 4, Section 3.1), but neither is established as a preregistered primary outcome.
The paper dates GPT-4o use to August 2024 but does not explicitly state the model’s release year; ai_tool.year is null rather than treating the experiment date as a release date.
The saved file is arXiv v1. The citation record identifies a later ACM version of record; differences in that version are unverified here.
notes: Extraction date: 2026-10-10. The PDF tables, figures, and Appendices A-E were inspected, the entire markdown conversion was read in consecutive chunks, and cited PDF pages were checked with pymupdf. Full-sample outcome-statistic inventory: novelty and usefulness each have only Figure 5 box plots and the shared all p > 0.05 statement in Section 5.2 (PDF pp. 8-9). Table 1 (PDF p. 7) supplies qualitative frame examples; Table 2 (PDF p. 13) supplies a qualitative hypothesis summary. Tables 3-9 concern prompts and the pre-task quiz; Tables 10-11 concern demographics. None supplies additional eligible effect statistics. All seven contrasts mapped at screening are retained for each outcome, including incomplete figure/qualitative records; only the pooled AI-versus-MANUAL records receive the printed p-value bound. This deliberately does not turn an omnibus/shared statement into invented pair-specific test results. The independent arms were randomized between people using a balanced Latin square (PDF p. 5, Section 4.1), not a crossover design. The quiz preceded assigned reframing, and the later expert-evaluation phase scored the already-produced assisted outputs, so it is not an after_ai outcome. Figure 8’s participant-count table has broken Unicode encoding in get_text(), and find_tables() does not recover it. Its explicit numeric cells were recovered from the embedded font glyph codes and verified against a pymupdf page rendering; no plot positions were used to infer outcome values. The rating observation is coded output because the paper says it analyzed the selected frames; each analyzed participant contributes one such output. The raters are not added to the randomized participant count. The study-level AI role is other because DIRECT and STRUCTURED supply ideas while FREE-FORM provides open chat. No shared sample with another paper is identified in the reconciled screening form. No across_people or after_ai outcome is reported.
